title: Giving surfaces a memory of contact

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Think of a stone step worn smooth in the middle. Nobody painted that wear on. It came from thousands of feet sliding across the same spot. Now, how would a video game or simulation reproduce that?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Usually an artist paints the scuffs by hand, I guess.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the gap Antoine's master's thesis at ÉTS tackles, under the direction of Sheldon Andrews, defended on August 14, 2026. A simulator's contact solver already computes impulses, sliding speed and friction. Then it moves the objects and forgets all that information.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. The idea is to give material maps, like color, roughness and normals, a persistent local memory of contact. Mechanical contact feeds the texture, exactly where contact happened.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How does it work step by step?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Sparse contact points are grouped into small local patches and projected into texture atlases. On a GPU grid, the system reconstructs tangential velocity, traction and frictional dissipation. Those fields drive how much sliding distance, dominant direction and wear accumulate, and the maps update progressively, with no remeshing of the model.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. First, a way to accumulate wear locally based on dissipation. Second, an architecture that projects contacts onto atlases and keeps the memory on a fixed mesh. Third, GelSight measurements from a controlled wear bench, used to build the Wear Surface Texture Datasets and compare simulated patterns with measured microgeometry.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two codebases. WearPaper holds the thesis sources, the article, the defense slides and the bibliography. TextureFriction is the interactive simulator, built with Qt six and OpenGL, with contact solving, GPU passes and wear atlases running in real time.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And do the results hold up?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: In the tested scenarios, the texels written track cumulative wear more closely than just how far a body traveled, and the contact shape changes the pattern. A cube or a torus on a plane stays within an interactive budget.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Where can people see the measurements?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The public dataset is on GitHub as WearSurfacesDatasets. The full write-up has the pipeline diagram and links to the related GraphQuon talk.
